paragraphs: A membership inference attack tries to determine whether a particular example appeared in a model’s training data. This paper investigates how learning causal relationships between inputs and outcomes can reduce that privacy risk, especially when the model encounters a different data distribution after training.

The authors first show that models learned using causal structure generalize better to unseen data, with particular benefits under distribution changes. They then use this generalization property to establish a theoretical connection between causal learning and privacy. Relative to models based on associations, the causal models offer stronger differential privacy guarantees and greater resistance to membership inference.

Experiments use simulated Bayesian networks and colored-MNIST. Across the tested distributions and sample sizes, attacks on associational models reach accuracy as high as 80%, while attacks on causal models perform close to random guessing. These findings support causal structure as a way to alleviate privacy attacks in the studied settings, connecting how a model generalizes with how much it reveals about training membership.
icml-2020-alleviating-privacy-attacks-vi.tldr: Learning causal relationships can improve generalization under distribution shifts and reduce vulnerability to membership inference attacks.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks often gain expressive power by stacking layers or processing a sequence in both directions. Stacking supports more complex nonlinear computations, while bidirectional processing lets predictions use information occurring later in the sequence. This paper examines whether delaying a single-layer network’s outputs can reproduce some of those benefits.

The proposed delayed-RNN leaves a gap between receiving an input and producing its corresponding output. The authors prove that a version with constrained weights is equivalent to a stacked recurrent network. Delaying outputs also permits partial access to later information, creating a form of the future context used by bidirectional networks.

In synthetic experiments, delayed-RNNs match bidirectional networks on some tasks requiring future information and outperform them on others. A natural language processing experiment also shows similar performance. Together, the results suggest that delayed networks can approximate stacked, bidirectional, and combined architectures with comparable or faster runtimes. The exact equivalence result applies to the weight-constrained construction; the broader architectural comparisons are supported by experiments.
icml-2020-approximating-stacked-and-bidi.tldr: Delaying a single-layer recurrent network’s outputs can reproduce stacking and approximate bidirectional processing with competitive performance and runtime.

paragraphs: Traditional differential privacy provides guarantees that do not depend on the data distribution. The authors argue that this can be a poor fit for machine learning, where a model is trained on a particular kind of data. Obtaining useful guarantees under the traditional formulation can substantially reduce prediction accuracy.

The paper introduces Bayesian differential privacy, which incorporates the data distribution into its privacy definition. It also develops a general method for accounting for privacy under this definition, building on the moments accountant. Together, the definition and accounting method provide a way to assess privacy while explicitly considering the distribution relevant to learning.

Experiments on datasets including MNIST and CIFAR-10 report substantially stronger guarantees for samples from the data distribution than traditional differential privacy would indicate, while classification accuracy remains high. The scope of that result matters: the improved guarantees concern in-distribution samples under the proposed formulation. The contribution is a distribution-aware approach to the privacy–accuracy tradeoff, supported by both accounting theory and empirical evaluation.
icml-2020-bayesian-differential-privacy-.tldr: Bayesian differential privacy incorporates the data distribution to obtain stronger in-distribution privacy guarantees while maintaining high classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Sequences can differ in length while still containing comparable patterns. This paper develops a Bayesian learning approach that handles such comparisons through Gaussian processes with signature kernels. The kernel serves as the covariance function, determining how the model relates different sequences while drawing on theoretical results from stochastic analysis.

Signatures represent sequential structure using tensors. Their computational size can grow unfavorably with both sequence length and the number of dimensions describing each observation. To address this scaling problem, the authors introduce a sparse variational method based on inducing tensors, providing an approximation designed specifically for the signature-based model.

The resulting Gaussian processes are also combined with LSTMs and GRUs to form larger models that bring together the strengths of these approaches. The authors benchmark them on classification datasets containing multivariate time series. The contribution connects a mathematically grounded way of comparing sequences with a computational approximation and recurrent neural components, making signature-based Bayesian learning applicable to richer sequential models.
icml-2020-bayesian-learning-from-sequent.tldr: Signature kernels, inducing tensors, and recurrent networks are combined to build scalable Gaussian-process models for sequential data.

paragraphs: Combining many decision trees can produce strong predictions, but understanding their joint behavior is harder than following a single tree. This paper studies how to replace an existing tree ensemble with one decision tree that reproduces its predictions exactly throughout the entire feature space.

The goal is to find the smallest tree satisfying that exact agreement requirement. The authors develop a dynamic programming algorithm that breaks the construction into recursive subproblems. Pruning and bounding rules reduce the number of recursive calls, making the search for an optimal replacement more manageable.

The algorithm produces optimal replacement trees for many datasets of practical interest. These classifiers are typically simpler and easier to interpret while preserving the ensemble’s behavior. The distinction between exact reproduction and approximate imitation is central: the replacement is required to agree beyond just the observed examples. This gives the work a clear interpretability objective—simplifying how predictions are represented without changing the predictions made by the original ensemble.
icml-2020-born-again-tree-ensembles-8f18.tldr: A dynamic programming method builds minimum-size decision trees that exactly reproduce a tree ensemble’s behavior across its feature space.

paragraphs: People’s preferences can depend on which alternatives they are offered, and different people may respond differently to the same menu. This paper asks how changing that menu can influence a group’s choices. It moves from predicting decisions with discrete choice models to optimizing the alternatives presented to decision-makers.

The framework considers three objectives: increasing agreement, increasing disagreement, and encouraging a particular choice. The authors show that these optimization problems are NP-hard in general, establishing a computational obstacle to solving every instance efficiently. They then examine restricted settings that reveal differences between the objectives.

Under some restrictions, promoting one option can be easier than making a group converge or divide. This distinguishes changing support for a particular alternative from reshaping agreement across the group. For the difficult problems, the authors develop approximation algorithms and report that they work well on real-world choice data. The result is both a framework for designing choice-set interventions and an account of where their computational difficulty arises.
icml-2020-choice-set-optimization-under-.tldr: Optimizing which choices a group sees is generally hard, but promoting one option can be easier than encouraging agreement or disagreement.

paragraphs: Molecular computing needs programming methods that fit chemical reactions and can operate where conventional electronics are unsuitable. This paper identifies a close connection between neural networks with binary weights and ReLU activations, known as BinaryConnect networks, and a class of coupled chemical reactions whose computations are robust to reaction rates.

The authors show how to train a BinaryConnect network using established deep learning optimization methods and then compile it into an equivalent chemical reaction network. This creates a route from a learned computational task to a chemical description. The rate independence of the resulting computation makes the approach a promising candidate for bioengineering implementation.

The paper illustrates the translation using IRIS and MNIST. It also generates a chemical reaction network for distinguishing virus types from gene expression levels. These examples demonstrate the proposed programming connection and its relevance to molecular tasks. The stated contribution is the compilation framework and generated reaction networks, establishing a path for transferring neural-network learning methods into molecular programming.
icml-2020-deep-molecular-programming-a-n.tldr: Trained binary-weight ReLU networks can be compiled into equivalent chemical reaction networks whose computations are independent of reaction rates.

paragraphs: Large image datasets often rely on crowdsourced collection because gathering rich data at scale is difficult. This paper uses human studies to examine what that process means for ImageNet. Its focus is how decisions made during dataset creation affect how faithfully the resulting benchmark represents image classification.

The analysis connects specific collection choices to biases that strong models exploit. It shows how noise in a collection pipeline can produce a systematic mismatch between a benchmark and the real-world task it is intended to represent. This makes the construction process relevant to interpreting model performance, rather than treating the dataset as a neutral measurement instrument.

The findings call for training and evaluation methods that account for this mismatch. Their significance is that progress on a benchmark needs to be understood in light of how its examples and labels were collected. The paper provides evidence that dataset design can shape what models learn and what benchmark success tells us about the broader task.
icml-2020-from-imagenet-to-image-classif.tldr: Human studies of ImageNet show how crowdsourced dataset design can introduce exploitable biases and misalign benchmark performance with the intended task.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often framed as keeping a prediction unchanged when an input changes slightly without changing its meaning. This paper examines the complementary failure: a small semantic change alters the correct label, but the model keeps its original prediction. In that case, the model is too invariant.

The authors demonstrate tradeoffs between these failure modes. Defenses targeting sensitivity-based attacks harm accuracy on invariance-based attacks in their investigation. They construct perturbations that adversarially trained and certifiably robust models resist, even though human labelers judge that the input’s class has changed. The prediction stability being protected is therefore itself responsible for an error.

The paper also formally connects excessively invariant classifiers to overly robust predictive features in standard datasets. Its findings show why resisting input changes is insufficient as a complete account of robustness: a useful classifier also needs to respond when the relevant meaning changes. The authors argue that new approaches are needed to address both kinds of adversarial examples.
icml-2020-fundamental-tradeoffs-between-.tldr: Defending against prediction changes can create excessive invariance, leaving models wrong when small input changes genuinely alter the correct class.

paragraphs: Often, a network is observed only after it has formed, leaving its construction process unknown. GraphOpt seeks to learn both a model of that formation process and a hidden objective that could explain the observed structure. Such an objective can provide an account of graph properties that transfers within a domain.

The framework treats adding links as a sequence of decisions. It uses maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning to discover an objective underlying those decisions, jointly learning an implicit formation model. A continuous latent action space helps the method scale while representing choices involved in constructing the graph.

Experiments show that the learned objective transfers across graphs with different characteristics. The learned stochastic policy also achieves competitive link prediction performance despite not being explicitly trained for that task, and it can construct graphs with properties resembling the observed graph. These findings support learning a reusable formation objective as a way to connect explanation, prediction, and graph generation within one framework.
icml-2020-graphopt-learning-optimization.tldr: GraphOpt learns a transferable hidden objective for sequential link formation, supporting graph explanation, link prediction, and graph generation.

paragraphs: In recommendation and online marketing, feedback may arrive long after an action, and some outcomes never produce an explicit signal. A purchase might eventually be recorded, while a decision not to buy remains unreported. This paper models that combination of random delay and permanently missing negative feedback using stochastic linear bandits.

The authors introduce OTFLinUCB and OTFLinTS, two computationally efficient algorithms that incorporate information as it arrives. Their design addresses the fact that an absent event can mean either that feedback is still delayed or that no positive event will occur. This makes partially observable delays central to the learning problem.

For OTFLinUCB, the paper proves an optimal regret bound of order d times the square root of T, with d representing dimension and T the time horizon, and examines dependence on delay-related parameters. Experiments with simulated and real data support the model, assumptions, and results. The contribution brings structured exploration to a feedback pattern that ordinary immediate-observation formulations do not capture.
icml-2020-linear-bandits-with-stochastic.tldr: Two efficient linear-bandit algorithms handle randomly delayed positive feedback and permanently censored outcomes, with an optimal regret bound for OTFLinUCB.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using data gathered under another policy. This paper studies that problem with function approximators for importance weights and value functions. These quantities provide two related ways to connect the observed data to the policy being evaluated.

The first estimator, MWL, directly learns importance ratios between state-action distributions, removing a reliance on knowing the behavior policy. The second, MQL, exchanges the roles of weights and value functions in the MWL construction. It can be interpreted as minimizing average Bellman errors and can be combined with MWL through a doubly robust approach.

The authors analyze sample complexity and establish asymptotic optimality in the tabular setting. They also investigate how the discriminator class affects the learned importance weights and explain connections among existing and new reinforcement learning algorithms. The contribution provides both new estimators and a unified theoretical perspective on learning weights and values for evaluation, with the tabular qualification attached specifically to the asymptotic optimality result.
icml-2020-minimax-weight-and-q-function-.tldr: MWL and MQL provide related approaches to off-policy evaluation through learned importance weights and value functions, backed by theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Multi-step greedy policies have been widely used when reinforcement learning has access to an environment model. This paper brings their benefits into model-free learning through two dynamic programming methods: kappa-policy iteration and kappa-value iteration. They update policies or value functions by repeatedly solving an auxiliary decision problem.

That auxiliary problem uses a shaped reward and a smaller discount factor. Existing reinforcement learning methods can solve it, including methods for discrete and continuous actions such as DQN and TRPO. This makes the approach a general construction around an underlying learning algorithm. The authors also identify an important parameter controlling how thoroughly each auxiliary problem is solved and suggest how to choose it.

Experiments on Atari and MuJoCo tasks show improvements over DQN and TRPO for an appropriate range of kappa. The findings support multi-step greedy updates as a way to improve existing learners, while making parameter choice part of the result. The reported gains depend on using a suitable range rather than holding uniformly across every setting.
icml-2020-multi-step-greedy-reinforcemen.tldr: Multi-step greedy updates can improve model-free reinforcement learning by repeatedly solving shaped auxiliary problems with existing algorithms.

paragraphs: Private synthetic data aims to replace a sensitive dataset with a sanitized version that approximately preserves answers to many statistical queries. This paper introduces three algorithms for that task. Each is computationally efficient when supplied with an optimization oracle, which can be implemented using existing non-private optimization tools such as integer programming solvers.

The paper separates the role of optimization quality from the privacy guarantee. How accurately the synthetic data preserves query answers depends on the oracle’s performance. Differential privacy, however, holds even in the worst case. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for accuracy and privacy for all three algorithms.

Empirical evaluations show good scaling as data dimensionality and the number of queries increase. In settings with large query workloads and strong privacy requirements, corresponding to small privacy-loss parameters, the methods outperform the High-Dimensional Matrix Mechanism in accuracy. The approach therefore offers a way to use powerful optimization software for private data release while retaining privacy protection independently of the optimizer’s success.
icml-2020-new-oracle-efficient-algorithm.tldr: Three private synthetic-data algorithms use optimization oracles to improve accuracy while guaranteeing privacy even when optimization performs poorly.

paragraphs: Learning from delayed outcomes becomes especially difficult when the environment changes before feedback arrives. For an online recommender optimizing long-term outcomes, observations may already describe an obsolete situation. The paper explains that learning can become impossible when environmental change occurs on a timescale comparable to the feedback delay.

The authors identify a condition under which immediate intermediate signals can help: after conditioning on those signals, the relationship to long-term behavior remains stationary. They formalize this setting as a stochastic bandit problem with environmental changes, delayed rewards, and intermediate observations. The signals provide a stable connection to eventual outcomes despite changes elsewhere in the system.

The paper develops an efficient algorithm based on UCRL and proves sublinear regret guarantees. Experiments show learning in changing, delayed environments where existing methods fail. The result depends on the stated stability condition for the intermediate signals. It demonstrates how appropriately informative early observations can make delayed learning possible in settings where the eventual feedback alone arrives too late.
icml-2020-non-stationary-delayed-bandits.tldr: Immediate intermediate signals enable learning with delayed rewards in changing environments when long-term behavior is stationary conditional on those signals.

paragraphs: Flat minima have been proposed as a way to understand why neural networks generalize. The idea concerns how much the training loss changes around a learned parameter setting. A difficulty is that existing flatness definitions can change when parameters are rescaled, making the measurement depend on parameter scale.

Earlier normalized measures attempted to remove that dependence by incorporating parameter scales. However, those adjustments lost a direct theoretical connection between flatness and generalization. This paper uses PAC-Bayesian analysis to provide generalization error bounds involving existing normalized flatness measures, restoring a theoretical basis for interpreting them.

The authors then use that analysis to introduce a new normalized flatness metric. They report that it has both a direct theoretical connection to generalization and a better empirical correlation with generalization error. The contribution addresses the measurement problem alongside the predictive usefulness of the metric: normalization is supported by error bounds, and the proposed measure is evaluated by how closely it tracks observed generalization.
icml-2020-normalized-flat-minima-explori.tldr: PAC-Bayesian analysis connects normalized flatness to generalization and motivates a new metric with improved empirical correlation to generalization error.

paragraphs: A game-playing agent can perform well against familiar opponents yet struggle against new ones. This paper studies that problem through two new games involving concealed information and non-transitive rewards, where strategic advantages can form cycles like rock-paper-scissors. Such settings require exploring a range of strategies rather than relying on one broadly dominant behavior.

The authors find that most current deep reinforcement learning methods explore these strategy spaces inefficiently and consequently generalize poorly. They propose a hierarchical agent whose upper level selects strategic responses to opponents and whose lower level translates those responses into primitive actions. The hierarchy is grounded in the game’s strategic structure.

That grounding helps assign credit across the hierarchy, linking outcomes to both strategic choices and their execution. In the reported experiments, the hierarchical agent generalizes to unseen opponents while conventional baselines fail to generalize. The findings support organizing behavior around opponent responses as a useful way to learn transferable strategies in the games studied.
icml-2020-options-as-responses-grounding.tldr: A hierarchy that selects and executes strategic responses helps agents generalize to unseen opponents in challenging multi-agent games.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can involve sensitive information when different users receive personalized decisions. This paper develops privacy-preserving exploration for episodic learning, motivated by settings such as personalized medicine. It formulates privacy using joint differential privacy, a variant designed for situations where each user receives their own outputs, including policy recommendations.

The authors introduce an optimism-based private learning algorithm with both PAC and regret guarantees. These capture complementary aspects of learning performance: obtaining sufficiently good behavior and controlling the accumulated cost of learning. The algorithm provides these guarantees while satisfying the proposed joint differential privacy requirement.

Compared with the non-private bounds, the privacy parameter appears only in lower-order terms. This supports the authors’ conclusion that privacy adds a moderate exploration cost within their analysis. The paper also derives lower bounds on sample complexity and regret under joint differential privacy. Together, these results characterize both an achievable learning performance and fundamental constraints on private episodic reinforcement learning, connecting privacy protection directly to the cost of exploration.
icml-2020-private-reinforcement-learning.tldr: An episodic reinforcement learning algorithm achieves joint differential privacy with PAC and regret guarantees whose privacy costs appear only in lower-order terms.

paragraphs: Standard supervised learning fits a model before seeing the inputs it will later predict. This paper asks whether knowing the next test input can improve its prediction. In linear prediction, the authors use that specific input to address bias introduced by regularization through techniques drawn from semi-parametric inference.

They first establish lower bounds on prediction error for ridge regression and the Lasso at the chosen test point. These bounds show that the methods must have substantial bias in certain test directions. The authors then develop two transductive prediction rules and provide finite-sample upper bounds on their error at that point.

Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate benefits from this targeted approach, particularly under distribution shift. The central idea is to make the next prediction problem part of the inference procedure, using the test input’s direction to combat regularization bias. The theoretical and empirical results show how a model’s general fitting objective can leave room for improvement when attention shifts to one specific upcoming prediction.
icml-2020-single-point-transductive-pred.tldr: Using the next test input during inference can reduce regularization bias in linear prediction, with particular benefits under distribution shift.

paragraphs: This paper develops two stochastic Gauss–Newton algorithms for a class of nonconvex problems whose objectives involve composed functions. It considers both objectives defined through expectations and those expressed as finite sums. Under standard assumptions, the methods approximate function values and Jacobians using classical stochastic estimators and SARAH estimators.

For the expectation setting, the authors establish an iteration complexity of order one over epsilon squared for reaching a stationary point in expectation, where epsilon specifies the desired accuracy. They also account for the total stochastic oracle calls needed to obtain function values and Jacobians. For finite sums, they provide the same order of iteration complexity and oracle-call estimates with high probability.

The distinction between iterations and oracle calls matters because each update requires information that has a computational cost. The authors identify their result as, to their knowledge, the first global stochastic oracle complexity analysis for these methods. Two numerical examples using synthetic and real datasets illustrate the theory. The convergence target is stationarity in a nonconvex problem.
icml-2020-stochastic-gauss-newton-algori.tldr: Two stochastic Gauss–Newton methods receive iteration and oracle-complexity guarantees for reaching stationarity in nonconvex compositional optimization.

paragraphs: Ranking metrics have a discrete structure that makes them difficult to optimize directly. StochasticRank addresses this problem with a framework aimed at the ranking metric itself. Its main tools are stochastic smoothing and a new gradient estimator derived using partial integration, providing a way to optimize an otherwise problematic loss.

The paper shows that conventional smoothing can introduce bias and develops a general correction for it. This matters because smoothing should make optimization tractable without silently changing the goal in an undesirable way. By adopting Stochastic Gradient Langevin Boosting, the authors also obtain a global convergence guarantee for their method.

The algorithm is implemented in CatBoost and outperforms existing approaches on several learning-to-rank datasets. Its scope extends beyond ranking to any scale-free discrete loss. The contribution therefore combines a treatment of smoothing bias, a gradient-estimation technique, and a convergence result with an implementation and empirical evidence. The global convergence claim is tied to the specified optimization approach used in the framework.
icml-2020-stochasticrank-global-optimiza.tldr: StochasticRank directly optimizes ranking metrics using corrected stochastic smoothing and gradient estimation, with global convergence through Langevin boosting.

paragraphs: Biomedical data often measures populations at several times without following the same individuals throughout. Reconstructing movement from those snapshots is challenging. Earlier optimal transport approaches match populations between pairs of times, but cannot represent the nonlinear paths common in the underlying dynamic systems considered by this paper.

TrajectoryNet connects continuous normalizing flows with dynamic optimal transport to model expected paths over time. A continuous flow can move one distribution into another, but the endpoints alone leave its route underconstrained. The method controls the continuous paths between distributions, making the trajectory itself an explicit part of the modeling problem.

The authors apply this approach to cellular dynamics measured through single-cell RNA sequencing. They report better interpolation of cellular distributions than recently proposed static optimal transport models. The result concerns expected movement inferred from population measurements: the model provides a continuous account of change between observed snapshots. Its contribution is to bring path structure into a setting where matching endpoints alone does not capture nonlinear dynamics.
icml-2020-trajectorynet-a-dynamic-optima.tldr: TrajectoryNet combines continuous flows with dynamic optimal transport to model nonlinear cellular paths between population snapshots.

paragraphs: Transfer learning usually adapts a pretrained model by changing its parameters. This paper proposes black-box adversarial reprogramming, or BAR, for situations where a model is available only through its input-output behavior. The aim is to reuse its learned capabilities for another task when data and computational resources are limited.

BAR combines zeroth-order optimization with multi-label mapping. It learns how to reprogram the model using only its responses, without knowing its architecture or modifying any model parameter. The approach draws on adversarial methods that influence predictions through input perturbations, applying that capability to transfer learning.

In limited-data experiments on autism spectrum disorder classification, diabetic retinopathy detection, and melanoma detection, BAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods and baseline transfer approaches. It also achieves performance comparable to adversarial reprogramming that requires complete model knowledge. These findings support the possibility of useful transfer through restricted prediction access, extending the reuse of trained models to settings where conventional fine-tuning is unavailable.
icml-2020-transfer-learning-without-know.tldr: BAR repurposes black-box models using only input-output responses, achieving strong transfer results on medical tasks with limited data.

paragraphs: A classifier needs a way to recognize inputs outside its training distribution. This paper introduces deterministic uncertainty quantification, or DUQ, which trains a single deep model to detect and reject such inputs using one forward pass. The approach builds on ideas from radial basis function networks.

The authors develop a new loss and a centroid update scheme to make this style of model train at scale while matching the accuracy of softmax models. They also add a gradient penalty that enforces detectability of input changes. This sensitivity constraint supports the model’s ability to identify unfamiliar data rather than producing uninformative responses to it.

The method scales to large datasets and matches or improves on Deep Ensembles for out-of-distribution detection in the reported comparisons. These include FashionMNIST versus MNIST and CIFAR-10 versus SVHN. The findings show that a carefully trained deterministic network can provide competitive detection with a single model and evaluation pass, connecting uncertainty behavior to the training objective and input sensitivity.
icml-2020-uncertainty-estimation-using-a.tldr: DUQ trains a single deterministic network to detect unfamiliar inputs in one forward pass, matching or improving on ensemble detection in reported tests.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder relies on an approximate posterior to represent latent variables given observed data. When that approximation poorly matches the true posterior, generative performance suffers. This paper expands the available family of approximations by allowing undirected graphical models, creating another way to represent relationships among latent variables.

The central technical contribution is an efficient training method for these undirected posteriors. The authors show that gradients of the training objective with respect to posterior parameters can be obtained by backpropagating through Markov chain Monte Carlo updates. This makes the sampling procedure part of the gradient computation used to learn the posterior.

They apply the gradient estimators to discrete variational autoencoders using Boltzmann machines as approximate posteriors. In the reported experiments, these undirected models outperform earlier results using directed graphical models. The contribution therefore joins a richer posterior modeling choice with a practical way to train it, and the empirical findings demonstrate its value for the discrete generative models studied.
icml-2020-undirected-graphical-models-as.tldr: Backpropagation through Monte Carlo updates enables undirected approximate posteriors that improve reported discrete VAE results over directed alternatives.
